Child with Puffy Eyes

local to the eye, or the first sign of edema everywhere · red flags · the dipstick splits the branches · minimal change diseaseDoes the swelling belong to the eye or to the whole child, and what does the urine dipstick show?

1Presentation2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Presentation
Bottom line
  • First decide whether the swelling is the eye's or the whole child's; check the airway and the orbit before anything else
  • Local swelling is allergy or infection; generalized edema means protein is lost or not made, or salt and water are retained
  • In the generalized branch the dipstick sorts it: 3+ to 4+ protein with no blood is nephrotic syndrome; blood or red cell casts, glomerulonephritis
What it is

Swollen lids, on one side or both

Sort by

Eye or whole child the urine: protein, blood, or clean

Hands off

Nephrotic syndrome, nephritis, anaphylaxis, the infected lid

2Urgent risks
AirwayStridor, wheeze or low blood pressure; swollen lips or tongue, or a hoarse voice

If there are hives or a likely allergen, choose intramuscular epinephrine first.

OrbitProptosis, pain with eye movement, blurred vision

If any orbital sign is present, choose CT of the orbits and sinuses, and IV antibiotics.

BellyEdema with fever, belly pain and rebound: spontaneous peritonitis

If a nephrotic child has peritoneal signs, choose cultures, then antibiotics.

PressureNephritis with a high pressure and headache, vomiting or confusion: hypertensive encephalopathy

If volume overload drives it, choose furosemide; nifedipine if it stays high.

ClotA nephrotic child with flank pain and hematuria, or one swollen leg: a clot
3Differential
Puffy eyes in a child, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Nephrotic syndrome
Minimal change diseaseThe filter loses its negative charge, so albumin leaks; it often follows a cold, an immunization or an insect bite. Prednisone daily for 4 to 6 weeks, then tapered; restrict salt. Give albumin with furosemide only when edema is severe: a diuretic alone can lower a plasma volume that is already low. Home urine dipstick: relapse is common and is treated with prednisone again. Pneumococcal and yearly influenza vaccines in remission; no live vaccines on high-dose steroids. During a relapse, watch for infection (spontaneous peritonitis, usually pneumococcal) from low immunoglobulin G, and for venous clots, the renal vein included, as antithrombin III is lost in the urine.		Both eyes, worst on waking; then the legs, belly and scrotumBlood pressure normal; 4+ protein without blood; albumin low Blood pressureLow oncotic pressure moves fluid into the tissues and leaves the plasma volume low, so the pressure stays normal; nephritis retains salt and water, so it rises.
Allergic conjunctivitis
Both eyes itchy and watery, ropey mucus; sneezing, clear runny nose; seasonalItch, and a clean urine
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (postinfectious glomerulonephritis)
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritisTreatment is supportive: salt and fluid restriction, and furosemide for volume overload; nifedipine when the pressure stays high. C3 is normal again by 8 weeks.		Puffy eyes with cola-colored urine; edema over daysBlood pressure high; about 1 to 3 weeks after strep throat, up to about 6 after impetigo; C3 low
Periorbital (preseptal) cellulitis
One red, warm, tender lid after a bite, scratch or sinusitisThe eye moves freely; normal vision, no proptosis
Orbital cellulitis
Fever, proptosis, pain with eye movementOphthalmoplegia or a change in vision; sinusitis is the usual source
Acute allergic reaction
Abrupt swelling of the lids, lips or tongueHives within minutes of a food, a drug or a sting
Hereditary angioedema
Hereditary angioedemaHereditary angioedema is autosomal dominant C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency; bradykinin, not histamine, causes the swelling, so angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors are contraindicated, and an attack does not answer to epinephrine: it is treated with C1 inhibitor concentrate or icatibant. Death is usually from airway swelling.		Recurrent swelling without hives; after dental work or stressLow C4; no response to epinephrine
Infectious conjunctivitis Conjunctivitis in the newbornGonococcal conjunctivitis at 2 to 5 days, with marked lid swelling and pus; chlamydial at 5 to 14 days, with mild swelling.Red eye, pus crusting the lids, mild lid swellingBegins in one eye; under 6, usually bacterial
Heart failure
Tires or breathes fast with activity; edema is uncommonBig liver, gallop, no protein in the urine
Liver failure or protein-losing enteropathyAscites with jaundice, or edema with chronic diarrheaLow albumin with a clean urine
Malnutrition (kwashiorkor)Edema with thin hair, poor growthDiet history
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Puffiness worst on waking, better by afternoonAllergy and edema alike: lying flat moves fluid to the lidsTest the urine
Tight shoes and waistband, pitting over the shins, scrotal or labial swelling, a fluid waveGeneralized edema and ascitesUrinalysis first
Dark circles under the eyes, a second crease below the lower lid, a bumpy conjunctivaAllergyAvoid the allergen; antihistamine eye drops
One red, tender lid; eye movements full and painless; vision normalPreseptal cellulitisOral antibiotics; recheck in 1 to 2 days
Dark urine about 1 to 3 weeks after a sore throat, or up to about 6 after skin soresGlomerulonephritisCreatinine, C3; antistreptolysin O or anti-deoxyribonuclease B

Pause point. The bait: allergy testing or orbit imaging for puffiness on both sides each morning. Waking puffiness separates neither allergy nor edema; the dipstick does.

Practice
  1. 5 yo boy with a week of puffy eyelids on both sides, worst when he wakes and better by afternoon, now with swollen ankles, a bigger belly, tiredness and a poor appetite; no itching, redness or discharge; blood pressure normal; urine dipstick 4+ protein and negative for blood → Minimal change disease → Nephrotic syndrome: protein without blood at a normal blood pressure
  2. 5 yo girl with 4 days of puffiness around both eyes, worst on waking; no itching, redness, discharge or fever; her shoes have felt tight since yesterday → Urinalysis → The dipstick shows whether the kidney is leaking protein
  3. 6 yo with hay fever and 5 days of puffy eyelids on both sides each morning, now with ankle swelling; a serum IgE level is high; no urine has been tested → It does not exclude a kidney cause → Atopy is common; the urine dipstick is still the next test
  4. 7 yo with puffy, itchy eyes on both sides every spring, clear watery discharge, sneezing and a runny nose; dark circles and an extra crease below both lower lids; afebrile; urine dipstick negative → Allergic conjunctivitis → Itch and a clean urine separate it from edema; antihistamine eye drops
  5. 3 yo whose eyelids and lips swell within 20 minutes of eating a cashew for the first time, with raised, itchy wheals on the chest; no hoarseness, wheeze or vomiting; blood pressure and oxygen saturation normal → IgE-mediated food allergy → Abrupt swelling with hives; hereditary angioedema brings no hives
  6. 4 yo with 2 days of swelling and redness of the right upper eyelid, which is warm and tender, around a scratch from the family cat; T 38.3 C; full, painless eye movements, normal vision, no proptosis → Periorbital cellulitis → One eye, warm and tender, orbit spared: oral antibiotics
  7. 4 yo with 2 days of a red left eye, thick yellow discharge and lids stuck together each morning, with mild lid puffiness; the eyelid skin is not red, warm or tender; afebrile; vision normal → Bacterial conjunctivitis → Pus and crusting; under 6, bacterial is more likely than viral
  8. 5 yo with puffy eyes and swelling of the ankles and scrotum; BP 96/58; urine dipstick 4+ protein, no blood; serum albumin 1.8 g/dL → Spot urine protein/creatinine ratio → Above 2 mg/mg with low albumin is nephrotic syndrome
  9. 3 yo with 2 weeks of puffy eyelids who tires after a few minutes of play and sweats and breathes fast with meals; RR 44, HR 150; liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin; gallop rhythm; urine dipstick negative for protein → Heart failure → Big liver and a gallop with a clean urine: echocardiogram next
  10. 2 yo with 3 weeks of swollen eyelids and legs and 2 months of loose stools; weight has fallen from the 50th to the 10th percentile; albumin 1.7 g/dL; urine dipstick negative for protein; bilirubin and INR normal → Protein-losing enteropathy → Albumin lost in the gut; stool alpha-1 antitrypsin is high
  11. 4 yo with periorbital and leg edema; BP 132/88; urinalysis 4+ protein with 30 red cells per high-power field; creatinine 1.1 mg/dL; C3 normal → Renal biopsy → Hematuria, hypertension and a high creatinine are atypical for minimal change disease
  12. 6 yo with minimal change disease that went into remission on prednisone, off steroids for 5 months; his home urine dipstick has shown 3+ to 4+ protein for 3 days and his eyes are puffy again; blood pressure normal, no blood in the urine → Restart daily prednisone → A relapse in a steroid-responsive child; relapses are common and do not harm the kidney
  13. 5 yo in a relapse of nephrotic syndrome, before steroids have been restarted, who develops pneumococcal peritonitis → Urinary loss of immunoglobulin and factor B → Opsonins for encapsulated organisms leak into the urine
  14. 5 yo with nephrotic syndrome in relapse and ascites, now with T 39.2 C, severe abdominal pain, guarding and rebound tenderness; HR 140, BP 90/54 → Cultures and IV antibiotics → Spontaneous peritonitis, usually pneumococcal; blood and peritoneal fluid cultures, then broad Gram-positive and Gram-negative cover
  15. 6 yo with severe nephrotic syndrome, albumin 1.4 g/dL, who develops sudden left flank pain, gross hematuria and an enlarged, palpable left kidney; creatinine has risen from 0.4 to 0.9 mg/dL; afebrile → Renal vein thrombosis → Urinary loss of antithrombin III and hemoconcentration; Doppler ultrasound
  16. 5 yo in week 3 of daily prednisone, 2 mg/kg, for a first episode of nephrotic syndrome; his kindergarten vaccines are due → Varicella vaccine → Live vaccines wait until the child is off high-dose steroids
  17. 5 yo discharged in remission from a first episode of minimal change disease; the parents ask how a relapse will be caught early → Home urine dipstick testing → Protein on the morning dipstick comes before the swelling
Pairs with Part I Proteinuria and Nephrotic Syndrome in a Child covers the lesion: minimal change disease versus membranous and FSGS (focal segmental glomerulosclerosis). It also covers starting steroids without a biopsy. Part II Hematuria and Nephritic Syndrome covers PSGN (poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis) and its C3 clock. Part II Anaphylaxis covers the acute allergic reaction and angioedema without hives. Part I Sinusitis and Its Complications covers preseptal versus orbital cellulitis and the orbital CT (computed tomography). Part I The Red Eye covers the conjunctivitis types.
Transferable rule For puffy eyes in a child, decide first whether the swelling belongs to the eye or to the whole child. If it is generalized, the urinalysis sorts it: protein alone means nephrotic syndrome, and blood with high blood pressure means nephritis.
Salient decoyPuffiness worst in the morning in an allergic child, treated as allergy without a urine dipstick.
Mirror twinPSGN also starts with puffy eyes; blood in the urine and a high blood pressure separate it.
Unchecked attributeA swollen lid called cellulitis without checking whether one eye or both, or whether the legs are swollen too.
Treat-the-numberFurosemide alone for nephrotic edema, when the plasma volume is already low.
